title: How to tell if a job reference is fake
summary: The candidate chooses the referee and supplies the contact details. How to check that a referee is real, reach them through a channel you found yourself, and…
body_markdown:
Check the referee without relying on the contact details the candidate supplied. Confirm from the company's website, its records or archived pages that the referee exists and worked there, reach them through the company's main number, and check whether their email domain and phone number belong to the company. A reference from a domain younger than the job, or from a number that leads back to the candidate, needs an explanation before you rely on it.


Find the company's main phone number yourself, on its website or in a directory, then call it and ask for the referee by name, or ask HR to confirm that the referee worked there. Let the referee describe the candidate's title, dates and work before you read out what the candidate claimed. The UK's National Protective Security Authority advises that telephone numbers supplied by the applicant "should not be wholly relied upon."


It is a reason to check further. New Zealand's Serious Fraud Office says written references from personal or free email accounts "can be a warning sign that the referee is not who they claim to be", and in one of its cases forged references came from personal accounts. Referees who have left a company, freelancers and staff at very small firms often have no work address, so confirm the referee through the company or their current employer.


That is a common policy and says nothing against the candidate. Acas describes a basic, or factual, reference as a short summary such as the employee's job title and the dates they worked there, and the NPSA notes that many employers only permit references to come from HR. Take the confirmed dates and title, ask HR whether your referee worked there and in what role, and find a second referee who can speak to the work.


Yes, and it has happened in documented cases. In a 2022 investigation summary, the Public Service Commission of Canada reported that a candidate admitted creating two email addresses "to impersonate and act as their own references." Reaching referees through the company, and not only through addresses the candidate supplied, is the check that catches it.


Yes. People Management reported in February 2026 that commercial reference houses offer paid-for references, employment verification, and even company email addresses and websites to support applications. A reference from such a service can pass a call to the number supplied, so check the company's registry record, the age of its domain and a footprint built by other people, and reach the referee through a number you found yourself.
